clue.text: The plumber's favourite instrument; it should hold 'a lot of tobacco

definitions.text: it should hold 'a lot of tobacco

explanation.surface: A plumber's beloved tool turns out to be a giant tobacco pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: Plumbers work with pipes, so their favourite music comes from pipes; split as 'bag' plus 'pipe' it is a smoker's pipe with a pouch-sized bowl.

clue.text: A lofting stroke in advance but unsuccessful

parts.note: a baff is an old golf stroke that strikes the ground to loft the ball
one who led was in front, in advance of the rest

explanation.surface: A golfer's high shot went ahead but failed.
explanation.walkthrough: A baff is an old golfing term for a stroke that sends the ball high.
explanation.definitionFit: Baffled means thwarted or frustrated, so efforts were unsuccessful.

parts.note: Tennyson's ballad The Revenge opens with an English commander lying at Flores in the Azores

explanation.surface: A man rested on an island in the Azores.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's 'The Revenge' begins 'At Flores in the Azores Sir Richard Grenville lay'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Richard Grenville, the Elizabethan sea captain, is the commander named in that opening line.

indicators.note: singers regrouped are put into a new order, so the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A choir rearranges itself and gets into the right mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in vein' sounds like 'in vain', but it points to the fluid in the veins of the Greek gods.
explanation.definitionFit: Ichor is the ethereal fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods instead of blood.

clue.text: Its prison, Byron wrote, was a holy place

definitions.text: Its prison, Byron wrote, was a holy place

parts.words: Its prison, Byron wrote, was a holy place
parts.note: Byron's sonnet on a Swiss lakeside castle begins by calling its prison a holy place

explanation.surface: A line from Byron about a sacred jail.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron's 'Sonnet on Chillon' says 'thy prison is a holy place'; the castle stands on Lake Geneva.
explanation.definitionFit: The castle on Lake Geneva where Bonivard was held, subject of Byron's poem The Prisoner of Chillon.

annotationWithheld.why: Can the oven be reconstructed ?: 'the oven be' rearranges into the composer's name with 'reconstructed' as the signal, but no word defines the answer

clue.text: Not so lachrymose when it goes to town

definitions.text: Not so lachrymose when it goes to town

parts.words: Not so lachrymose when it goes to town
parts.note: a word for one more given to weeping becomes, set before 'town', the official who calls out announcements

explanation.surface: Someone who weeps less once they get to the city.
explanation.walkthrough: The town crier shouts the news and is not tearful at all; 'lachrymose' plays on crying as weeping.
explanation.definitionFit: A crier is one who cries out, and a town crier calls public announcements.

parts.note: steam locomotives emit their own clouds of smoke, as a self-promoter writes their own praise

explanation.surface: Self-publicists who write their own good reviews.
explanation.walkthrough: A puff is a piece of puffery; here it is a burst of steam from a locomotive.
explanation.definitionFit: Steam engines give out puffs of steam and smoke as they run.

clue.text: " To-morrow to woods and pastures new ' (Milton)

definitions.text: " To-morrow to woods and pastures new ' (Milton)

parts.words: " To-morrow to woods and pastures new ' (Milton)
parts.note: the closing line of Milton's Lycidas, with one adjective missing before 'woods'

explanation.surface: A quotation from Milton with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line of Lycidas runs 'Tomorrow to fresh woods, and pastures new'; the blank printed in the paper is lost in the text here.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Milton's line describes the woods as new and unvisited.

clue.text: The fiance should exemplify this place of combat

parts.note: a newly engaged woman is a prized catch and wears a ring, so she is a prized ring

explanation.surface: A bride-to-be is held up as a model of something.
explanation.walkthrough: A boxing arena is a prize ring; the engaged woman, valued and given a ring, is 'prized' and 'ring' in another sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A prize ring is the roped square where prizefighters box.

clue.text: Bacon's companion takes an interest in football here

parts.note: liver and bacon is a classic British dish, so liver accompanies bacon
the football pools are a British betting game on match results, and a pool is a stake in it

explanation.surface: Sir Francis Bacon's friend develops an interest in the beautiful game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bacon' looks like the philosopher, but it is the breakfast meat; 'here' is the definition, pointing to a city famous for football.
explanation.definitionFit: The English port city is home to two famous football clubs, so it is a place where football interest runs high.

clue.text: One can find her on the marshes

definitions.text: One can find her on the marshes

indicators.note: the bird is found spelled out across the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A woman can be spotted out on the marshland.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird's name runs straight through 'her on'; the whole clue then describes a wading bird of the marshes.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-legged grey wading bird that stalks fish in marshes and reed beds.

parts.note: the old ballad's refrain says Greensleeves was all the singer's joy and their heart of gold

explanation.surface: A singer claims the lady of the old ballad as their own.
explanation.walkthrough: The refrain of Greensleeves runs 'Greensleeves was all my joy, Greensleeves was my delight'.
explanation.definitionFit: A delight is a source of great pleasure, which is what the singer calls the lady.

clue.text: Would shaving prevent one becoming it ?

definitions.text: Would shaving prevent one becoming it ?

parts.words: Would shaving prevent one becoming it ?
parts.note: an old man is named for his grey whiskers, which a razor would remove

explanation.surface: Asking whether a razor can stop old age.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaving removes the beard but not the years, so it cannot stop anyone growing old.
explanation.definitionFit: A graybeard is an old man, named for the grey whiskers of age.

parts.note: to lack something is to have none of it, giving the word for none
a vice is a tool that grips work on a bench

explanation.surface: An explanation of why learners cannot hold on to anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grip' leads to the workshop tool, plural to match the beginners; 'Showing why' joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Novices are people new to an activity, as beginners are.

parts.note: smooth running is measured against a mechanism, as in 'going like' it

explanation.surface: The standard by which progress is judged.
explanation.walkthrough: Things that go perfectly are said to go 'like clockwork', so the mechanism is the yardstick for going well.
explanation.definitionFit: Clockwork is the spring-driven mechanism of a clock, the byword for regular smooth running.

explanation.surface: Something resembling a mask opens a book.
explanation.walkthrough: A mask sits before the face, so read as 'pre-face' the word suits a mask; it is also the opening section of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A preface is the introductory text before a book's main body; a mask goes in front of the face.

parts.note: a scheme is a plan
Ted is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Edward's scheme for laying out a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden is set with flowers and shrubs that have been put into the ground.

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at a speeding train.
explanation.definitionFit: To express is to put into words, and an express is a fast train with few stops.

clue.text: But the president wasn't so green

definitions.text: But the president wasn't so green

parts.words: But the president wasn't so green
parts.note: a US president shares his name with a shade of green worn by Robin Hood's men

explanation.surface: Defending an American president against charges of naivety.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln green is the forest cloth of Robin Hood, and Abraham Lincoln was no innocent; 'green' plays on both colour and naivety.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham Lincoln was a US president, and his surname is also a shade of green cloth.

parts.note: the letters of the answer, rearranged, spell the word 'conical'

explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse anagram: rearranging the answer gives 'conical'; the clue itself is suitably short of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic means using very few words, and the clue is terse to match.

explanation.surface: Endless promotion for a minor political party.
explanation.walkthrough: Lib stands for Liberal, by the 1950s a small party in British politics.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad lib means without limit or restraint, as much as one likes.

explanation.surface: Asking who might be the goddess of singing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thora' is a popular Victorian ballad by Stephen Adams, and the name reads as a feminine form of the Norse god Thor.

clue.text: Of which a German soothsayer might have warned Caesar

definitions.text: Of which a German soothsayer might have warned Caesar

parts.words: Of which a German soothsayer might have warned Caesar
parts.note: the soothsayer said 'Beware the Ides of March', and in German 'the Ides' would start with 'der'

explanation.surface: Imagining Julius Caesar's fortune-teller speaking German.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'der Ides', the word is what a German soothsayer would tell Caesar to beware; the definition is a mocks-and-scorns sense the solver must supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocks and scorns; split into 'der' and 'Ides' it is German for the fatal day in March.

explanation.surface: Someone made a remark and then expired.
explanation.definitionFit: To croak is to speak in a hoarse voice, and slang for to die.
